title: Two Ways Parent of Origin Matters

scenes.visual: Title card 'Two Ways Parent of Origin Matters' over two carried inheritance lanes. Reuse the first film's COLOUR MAP: maternal chromosomes and organelles = TEAL; paternal chromosomes and allele tags = GOLD; white-eye allele = WHITE; red-eye allele = RED; Y chromosome and inactive marks = GREY. New accent: expressed output = GREEN. All cells and organelles are labelled cartoons marked 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: The first film followed an allele because it sat on the X. Can parent of origin matter beyond the sex chromosomes? It can, in two different ways. The key is to ask whether transmission or expression changed.
scenes.caption: The first film followed an allele because it sat on the X. Can parent of origin matter beyond the sex chromosomes? It can, in two different ways. The key is to ask whether transmission or expression changed.
scenes.visual: The first film's X-shaped route map shrinks to the upper left. A large egg and sperm appear center frame. Two question lanes unfold beneath them: 'Which DNA arrives?' and 'Which allele acts?'
scenes.narration: The first film followed an allele because it sat on the X. Can parent of origin matter beyond the sex chromosomes? It can, in two different ways. The key is to ask whether transmission or expression changed.

scenes.tts: In the first lane, organelle inheritance changes which DNA arrives. In the second, genomic imprinting changes which parental nuclear allele is expressed. Keep transmission and expression separate. Both mechanisms make pedigrees depend on parent, but for different physical reasons.
scenes.caption: In the first lane, organelle inheritance changes which DNA arrives. In the second, genomic imprinting changes which parental nuclear allele is expressed. Keep transmission and expression separate. Both mechanisms make pedigrees depend on parent, but for different physical reasons.
scenes.visual: The two lanes widen to fill the frame. TEAL mitochondrion cartoons move through the upper lane labelled 'transmission'. Paired TEAL and GOLD chromosome blocks move through the lower lane labelled 'expression'.
scenes.narration: In the first lane, organelle inheritance changes which DNA arrives. In the second, genomic imprinting changes which parental nuclear allele is expressed. Keep transmission and expression separate. Both mechanisms make pedigrees depend on parent, but for different physical reasons.

scenes.tts: Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry small genomes outside the nucleus. An egg supplies abundant cytoplasm and organelles. A male gamete usually contributes far less cytoplasm. That difference gives maternal organelles an enormous numerical head start.
scenes.caption: Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry small genomes outside the nucleus. An egg supplies abundant cytoplasm and organelles. A male gamete usually contributes far less cytoplasm. That difference gives maternal organelles an enormous numerical head start.
scenes.visual: A large TEAL egg fills the upper lane with many labelled mitochondrion and chloroplast blocks. A small GOLD sperm enters with a large nuclear block and little cytoplasm. No molecular structures are drawn.
scenes.narration: Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry small genomes outside the nucleus. An egg supplies abundant cytoplasm and organelles. A male gamete usually contributes far less cytoplasm. That difference gives maternal organelles an enormous numerical head start.

scenes.tts: Many species also exclude, deplete, or destroy paternal organelles or their DNA. Organelle genomes are therefore generally inherited from the mother. The mother's organelle pattern reaches sons and daughters. Some species instead show paternal or biparental organelle transmission.
scenes.caption: Many species also exclude, deplete, or destroy paternal organelles or their DNA. Organelle genomes are therefore generally inherited from the mother. The mother's organelle pattern reaches sons and daughters. Some species instead show paternal or biparental organelle transmission.
scenes.visual: Three small alternative species panels branch from GOLD paternal organelles, labelled 'excluded', 'depleted', or 'destroyed'; each is marked 'schematic'. The TEAL maternal organelles divide into daughter and son offspring. A scope label remains: 'generally maternal; exceptions occur'.
scenes.narration: Many species also exclude, deplete, or destroy paternal organelles or their DNA. Organelle genomes are therefore generally inherited from the mother. The mother's organelle pattern reaches sons and daughters. Some species instead show paternal or biparental organelle transmission.

scenes.tts: Both sexes can inherit a maternal organelle variant. Each child now carries the mother's organelle DNA. But carrying a variant is not the same as passing it on.
scenes.caption: Both sexes can inherit a maternal organelle variant. Each child now carries the mother's organelle DNA. But carrying a variant is not the same as passing it on.
scenes.visual: A three-generation pedigree grows across the upper lane. TEAL organelles enter a daughter and a son. The next generation's row stays blank, with no paths drawn into it yet.
scenes.narration: Both sexes can inherit a maternal organelle variant. Each child now carries the mother's organelle DNA. But carrying a variant is not the same as passing it on.

scenes.tts: Imprinting is different. An imprinted gene is nuclear. Both parents transmit a copy, but only one parental copy is expressed. A parent-of-origin mark decides which. The mark does not change the DNA sequence. The marks are set during egg or sperm formation, then reset in the next generation.
scenes.caption: Imprinting is different. An imprinted gene is nuclear. Both parents transmit a copy, but only one parental copy is expressed. A parent-of-origin mark decides which. The mark does not change the DNA sequence. The marks are set during egg or sperm formation, then reset in the next generation.
scenes.visual: Focus shifts to the lower lane. TEAL maternal and GOLD paternal chromosome blocks enter the same nucleus. Identical gene rectangles align. A GREY reversible tag covers one output arrow while the DNA rectangles remain visually identical.
scenes.narration: Imprinting is different. An imprinted gene is nuclear. Both parents transmit a copy, but only one parental copy is expressed. A parent-of-origin mark decides which. The mark does not change the DNA sequence. The marks are set during egg or sperm formation, then reset in the next generation.

scenes.tts: Both a daughter and a son inherit the same maternal organelle variant. Each carries it. Which child can place that variant into the next generation's eggs? Trace the lineage, not the child's own phenotype. The question is about transmission, not expression.
scenes.caption: Both a daughter and a son inherit the same maternal organelle variant. Each carries it. Which child can place that variant into the next generation's eggs? Trace the lineage, not the child's own phenotype. The question is about transmission, not expression.
scenes.visual: A daughter and son each hold the same TEAL organelle badge. Their paths approach a blank next generation. Question card: 'Who can continue the organelle lineage through eggs?' The lower imprinting lane stays neutral.
scenes.narration: Both a daughter and a son inherit the same maternal organelle variant. Each carries it. Which child can place that variant into the next generation's eggs? Trace the lineage, not the child's own phenotype. The question is about transmission, not expression.

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Hold the daughter and son with their TEAL organelle badges, the blank next generation and the question card 'Who can continue the organelle lineage through eggs?'. The imprinting lane stays neutral; a quiet ring timer completes one turn.

scenes.tts: The daughter can usually pass it through eggs into another generation. The son can carry the variant, but his sperm usually do not transmit those organelles. The children can therefore share a variant while only one sex continues its lineage.
scenes.caption: The daughter can usually pass it through eggs into another generation. The son can carry the variant, but his sperm usually do not transmit those organelles. The children can therefore share a variant while only one sex continues its lineage.
scenes.visual: The daughter's TEAL path continues through a large egg into the next generation. The son's TEAL path ends before a sperm icon, without a rejection symbol. A label reads 'usual maternal pattern; exceptions occur'.
scenes.narration: The daughter can usually pass it through eggs into another generation. The son can carry the variant, but his sperm usually do not transmit those organelles. The children can therefore share a variant while only one sex continues its lineage.

scenes.tts: Now compare the lanes. Organelle inheritance usually filters transmission through the egg. Imprinting transmits both nuclear copies, then filters expression by parental origin. These mechanisms can produce different pedigrees.
scenes.caption: Now compare the lanes. Organelle inheritance usually filters transmission through the egg. Imprinting transmits both nuclear copies, then filters expression by parental origin. These mechanisms can produce different pedigrees.
scenes.visual: Both lanes return side by side. Upper lane: only TEAL organelle DNA enters. Lower lane: TEAL and GOLD nuclear copies both enter, but one GREEN output arrow remains. Large labels transform from 'which arrives?' to 'which acts?'
scenes.narration: Now compare the lanes. Organelle inheritance usually filters transmission through the egg. Imprinting transmits both nuclear copies, then filters expression by parental origin. These mechanisms can produce different pedigrees.

scenes.tts: Inheritance patterns depend on allele identity, chromosome location, and parental origin. Here, parent of origin can decide which DNA arrives or which allele acts. Most nuclear genes use both parental copies, so imprinting is a special case.
scenes.caption: Inheritance patterns depend on allele identity, chromosome location, and parental origin. Here, parent of origin can decide which DNA arrives or which allele acts. Most nuclear genes use both parental copies, so imprinting is a special case.
scenes.visual: The three-part ledger from the first film returns. 'Parental origin' glows, then branches to 'transmission' and 'expression'. A broad background row labelled 'most nuclear genes: both copies used' stays visible behind a smaller 'imprinted subset'.
scenes.narration: Inheritance patterns depend on allele identity, chromosome location, and parental origin. Here, parent of origin can decide which DNA arrives or which allele acts. Most nuclear genes use both parental copies, so imprinting is a special case.

scenes.tts: When a pedigree depends on the mother, ask what is moving. Is organelle DNA traveling through eggs? Or are both nuclear alleles present while a parental mark controls expression?
scenes.caption: When a pedigree depends on the mother, ask what is moving. Is organelle DNA traveling through eggs? Or are both nuclear alleles present while a parental mark controls expression?
scenes.visual: A pedigree icon splits into the two familiar lanes. A magnifying glass alternates between TEAL organelles in an egg and paired nuclear alleles with one GREY tag. The labels 'transmitted' and 'expressed' settle beneath them.
scenes.narration: When a pedigree depends on the mother, ask what is moving. Is organelle DNA traveling through eggs? Or are both nuclear alleles present while a parental mark controls expression?

scenes.visual: End card with one line only: 'Parent of origin can decide which DNA arrives or which allele acts.'
